headline: Japanese officials have called a wave of hacks on more than 20 major companies an emergency, and experts say AI may be making such attacks easier.
score_reason: Pool score 7 lowered by 1: AI's role is suspected by experts, not shown, and the Japan wave was already covered in our 9 Oct edition.
importance_line: Customers of the affected Japanese companies face a higher risk of fraud after the leaks and regulators are reportedly tightening identity checks, but experts only suspect AI is involved and no attack has been explicitly linked to it.
summary: The Financial Times reports, as relayed by PCMag, that more than 20 major Japanese companies, including the convenience-store chain Lawson and the car-rental firm Times Car, have reported attacks that lost tens of millions of pieces of customer data, among them 1.67 million email addresses from the booking system of rail operator JR East, and Japan's cybersecurity minister, Toshiharu Furukawa, called the situation "extremely critical". Experts quoted by the FT and Reuters say AI may be lowering the effort needed to attack smaller targets, although the attacks have not been explicitly linked to AI; this continues the Japan coverage of our 9 Oct 2026 edition, which carried Reuters on hacks in South Korea and Japan.
notes: Read on PCMag (the pool item is the PCMag Middle East copy, which adds a Middle East paragraph; the US page, dated 10 Oct 2026, carries the same text). PCMag relays The Financial Times and Reuters, so the FT is credited as first reporter and the link goes to the page where the text was read; the FT and Reuters originals were not opened. Head of the National Cybersecurity Strategy Headquarters Masaaki Taira called it an 'emergency in cyberspace'.
